1.title: Enforcement, Handoffs and Hooks
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Enforcement, Handoffs and Hooks. This module covers task statements one point four and one point five: enforcement, handoffs and hooks. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) versus prompt-based guidance. When a rule needs deterministic compliance, and why prompts alone have a non-zero failure rate. Prerequisite gates that block a tool until an earlier step has finished. Structured handoffs when the agent escalates to a person. Hooks: Post Tool Use to normalize results, and call interception to block policy violations.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply Stops Wrong Refunds
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply Stops Wrong Refunds. In nine percent of conversations the support agent calls process refund without first verifying the customer with get customer. Some refunds went to the wrong account. The team has already written "A L W A Y S verify the customer first" in the system prompt; the problem continues.

1.title: Enforcement Versus Guidance
1.text: Enforcement Versus Guidance. How it works. Prompt-based guidance: Instructions, rules and examples in the prompt. Programmatic enforcement: Code outside the model: hooks and prerequisite gates. Reliability. Prompt-based guidance: Probabilistic: the model usually complies, but not always. Programmatic enforcement: Deterministic: the code runs every time. Use when. Prompt-based guidance: Style, preferences, soft ordering. Programmatic enforcement: Identity checks before money moves, hard limits, legal or financial rules. When errors have financial or legal consequences, "usually" is not enough. A prompt has a non-zero failure rate; more emphasis or more examples reduce it but never remove it.

1.title: Enforcement Versus Guidance, continued
1.text: Enforcement Versus Guidance, continued. The figure shows this: Prompt guidance is probabilistic; programmatic enforcement (hooks and prerequisite gates) is deterministic and is the answer when compliance must be guaranteed. Exam tip: Requirement says "must", "always", "guarantee", money, identity or compliance? to programmatic enforcement. Answers that only strengthen the prompt, add few-shot examples or filter which tools exist are probabilistic or off-target.

1.title: Prerequisite Gates and Multi-Concern Requests
1.text: Prerequisite Gates and Multi-Concern Requests. Prerequisite gate: the code blocks a downstream tool call until the prerequisite step has completed. Example: process refund and lookup order stay blocked until get customer has returned a verified customer I D. The gate can live in the tool wrapper (check shared state) or in a hook (next section). The model sees a clear message such as "verify the customer first" and corrects itself. Multi-concern requests ("my order is late and I was charged twice"): decompose the message into separate items, investigate each in parallel using shared context (for example the verified customer), then synthesize one unified resolution.

1.title: Structured Handoffs to Humans
1.text: Structured Handoffs to Humans. When the agent escalates, the human agent usually cannot see the conversation transcript. So the agent compiles a structured handoff summary.

1.title: Structured Handoffs to Humans, continued
1.text: Structured Handoffs to Humans, continued. The figure shows this: A structured handoff summary for a human agent: customer I D, root cause, amount, what was tried, and the recommended action.

1.title: Structured Handoffs to Humans, continued
1.text: Structured Handoffs to Humans, continued. Customer I D. C-forty-eight thousand two hundred thirteen (verified). Root cause. Carrier damaged the parcel; photo evidence attached. Amount. Refund of one hundred eighty-nine dollars and zero cents requested. Actions taken. Order located, return policy checked, refund blocked by the limit rule. Recommended action. Approve a full refund and send a replacement. Exam tip: A handoff should be self-contained and structured, not "see transcript" and not a free-text paragraph.

1.title: Hooks
1.text: Hooks. Hooks are code that the S D K (software development kit) runs at fixed points of the agent loop, outside the model. Two patterns matter for the exam.

1.title: Hooks, continued
1.text: Hooks, continued. The figure shows this: Where hooks act: intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce rules, and intercept tool results to normalize data before the model processes it.

1.title: Hooks, continued
1.text: Hooks, continued. Tool-result hook (Post Tool Use). What it does: Transforms the result before the model reads it. Example: Normalize Unix timestamps, I S O eighty-six oh one dates and numeric status codes from different M C P (Model Context Protocol) tools into one format. Tool-call interception (before the tool runs). What it does: Inspects the outgoing call and can block it or redirect it. Example: Block process refund for amounts above five hundred dollars and send the case to human escalation. Deterministic guarantee (hook) versus probabilistic compliance (prompt): choose a hook when a business rule must hold every time.

1.title: Hooks, continued
1.text: Hooks, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Hooks, continued
1.text: Hooks, continued. In current documentation, the call-interception hook is the Pre Tool Use event: it can deny a call (permission Decision: "deny", or exit code two for shell hooks) with a reason that Claude sees, and can rewrite arguments with updated Input. The result hook is Post Tool Use: the tool has already run, so it cannot prevent the call, but it can replace the result with updated Tool Output. Hooks are registered in the S D K hooks option (matcher such as "Bash" or "mcp server tool") or in settings files. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Choose the hook by what it acts on: the outgoing call (block or redirect) or the incoming result (normalize). A rule about money or identity is a call hook.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Enforce versus guide: Hard rules (money, identity, compliance) to hooks or gates; soft style to prompt. Why prompts fall short: Non-zero failure rate; more emphasis only lowers the odds. Prerequisite gate: Block process refund or lookup order until get customer returns a verified I D. Multi-concern request: Decompose to investigate in parallel with shared context to one unified answer. Handoff: Structured: customer I D, root cause, amount, actions taken, recommended action. Post Tool Use hook: Normalizes results (timestamps, I S O dates, status codes) before the model reads them. Interception hook: Blocks or redirects calls (refund greater than five hundred dollars to human); event Pre Tool Use in current docs.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Birchwood's agent sometimes calls process refund before verifying the customer. The system prompt already says verification is mandatory. What change most effectively fixes this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A required order for a financial operation needs deterministic enforcement. Prompt wording and examples stay probabilistic, and fewer tools do not control order.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A mobile app sends refund amounts, and policy says refunds over five hundred dollars must be approved by a person. Which design guarantees the policy? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A hook enforces the threshold every time and can redirect to the right workflow. The others rely on the model following instructions.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Three M C P tools return dates as Unix timestamps, I S O eighty-six oh one strings and "month, day, year" text, and the agent mixes up the order of events. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A result-transforming hook gives the model consistent data deterministically, before it reads it.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. When the agent escalates, support staff complain they cannot tell what was already done. The staff cannot open the chat transcript. What should the agent produce? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Humans who cannot see the transcript need a structured, self-contained handoff to act on.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A customer writes: "My package is late and I see a duplicate charge." What is the best way to handle the two concerns? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Decompose, investigate in parallel using shared context, then synthesize a single resolution.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which statement about hooks versus prompts is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Hook code runs every time, so it gives deterministic guarantees; prompt instructions can be skipped with a small but non-zero probability.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which requirement is the best candidate for a prompt instruction, not a hook? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Tone is a soft preference where small variation is acceptable. The other three are hard rules that need enforcement.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Select two. Which two requirements should be enforced in code with a hook or gate rather than only in the prompt? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Identity checks before money moves and hard monetary limits are non-negotiable rules that need deterministic enforcement. Tone, brevity and optional links are soft preferences.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two items belong in a structured handoff to a human agent? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. A handoff must be self-contained: identifiers and findings the human needs to act. A raw transcript or a mood word does not help, and asking the customer again wastes their time.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: B. Question two: B. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: C. Question eight: B and D. Question nine: C and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
